program_meta.program_name: Ph.D. in Machine Learning (Machine Learning Department, MLD) and Ph.D. in Computer Science (Computer Science Department, CSD) — both in the School of Computer Science (SCS). One SCS graduate application covers both; you may apply to up to three doctoral programs on it.
program_meta.sop_limit: No word count published. SCS-wide instruction, verbatim: "Each program has specific requirements for the Statement of Purpose, detailed on the application. Generally: You should prepare a concise one- or two-page essay that describes your research interests, related experiences and objectives in pursuing a graduate degree at Carnegie Mellon." So plan for 1-2 pages (~700-1100 words). The exact per-program limit is only shown inside the application form once it opens Sept 9, 2026 — re-check then. SCS also states verbatim: "We recommend that you use AI tools only in a limited fashion... Remember that you are solely responsible for 100% of what is submitted in your application."
program_meta.extra_essays: No separate diversity/personal statement is listed for the MLD or CSD Ph.D. SCS notes that "Some of our programs request a 'live' video essay or prerecorded digital portfolio" (1-3 minutes) — this is generally a master's-program requirement, not stated for MLD/CSD Ph.D. Program-specific questions appear inside the application. A resume/CV is required.
program_meta.deadline_fall_2027: Application opens Sept. 9, 2026. Early deadline: Nov. 18, 2026 (3 p.m. EST) — cost saving only, NOT early decision. Final deadline: Dec. 9, 2026 (3 p.m. EST). Recommenders have until Dec. 9, 2026 even if you submit early. SCS strongly recommends taking/retaking GRE or TOEFL/IELTS/Duolingo no later than Nov. 25, 2026.
program_meta.lor_count: Three (3) required; the application allows up to five; no more than five accepted. At least two should be from faculty or recent employers; SCS explicitly wants writers who can speak to your ability to do independent research.
program_meta.gre: Optional. MLD Ph.D. page states verbatim: "GRE scores are OPTIONAL. The committee uses GRE scores to gauge quantitative skills, and to a lesser extent, also verbal skills." CSD Ph.D. lists "Graduate Record Exam (GRE) (optional)". Scores older than five years are not accepted. Codes: Institution 2074, Department 0402.
program_meta.english_test: REQUIRED for Akshat — NO India / English-medium exemption. SCS verbatim: "We do not issue waivers for non-native speakers of English. In particular, we do not issue waivers based on previous study at a U.S. high school, college or university. We also do not issue waivers based on previous study at an English-language high school, college or university outside of the United States. No amount of educational experience in English, regardless of the country it occurred in, will result in a test waiver." CSD adds verbatim: "The Computer Science Department cannot issue waivers and does not have any events or pre-admit programs that would qualify an applicant for a fee or language waiver." Accepted: TOEFL (preferred), IELTS, or Duolingo. Score must be no older than two years (nothing taken before Sept. 1, 2024). Typical admitted ranges: TOEFL iBT 105-114, IELTS 7-8, Duolingo 130-155. TOEFL codes: Institution 4256, Department 78.
program_meta.app_fee: USD $100 per program; discounted to USD $80 per program if submitted before the early deadline of Nov. 18, 2026 (3 p.m. EST). Credit card only. Financial-hardship fee waivers are available within the application; CSD itself cannot issue them.
program_meta.advisor_model: Department admission, advisor matched after admission. CSD verbatim: "You are not expected to have an advisor before applying for the doctoral program... The application provides the opportunity to select Computer Science Department faculty who you believe align with your research area(s). Official advisor matching occurs after you are admitted to the program." MLD operates the same way (admitted to the department, advisor settled in the first year) — MEDIUM confidence, not restated verbatim on the MLD page in this pass. Practical implication: naming 2-4 specific faculty in the SOP matters, but you are not applying to one person's lab. All admitted CSD Ph.D. students get full funding (stipend, tuition, fees, health insurance), identical for domestic and international students.
program_meta.ms_research_access: CMU's research-oriented master's options, ranked for a PhD-bound applicant: (1) MSR — Master of Science in Robotics (Robotics Institute) — thesis-based research degree, the most research-native SCS master's; (2) MSCS — Master of Science in Computer Science (CSD) — research-oriented with a thesis pathway; (3) MSML — Master's in Machine Learning (MLD), plus a separate 'MS in Machine Learning - Advanced Study' variant — MLD-run and research-flavoured but small and expensive; (4) MSAII — Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence and Innovation (LTI) — a professional/industry-facing degree, the WEAKEST fit for a research-oriented applicant. RECOMMENDATION for Akshat: apply directly to the Ph.D. (MLD and/or CSD). If a master's backstop is wanted, MSR or MSCS give real thesis access; do not use MSAII as a PhD springboard. NOTE: degree-page details for MSR/MSCS/MSAII were not individually opened in this pass — MEDIUM confidence on the ranking, HIGH confidence that MLD/CSD Ph.D. is the correct primary target.
program_meta.notes: One SCS online application covers most SCS graduate programs; you may apply to up to three doctoral programs and any master's programs (fee is per program). The 'ML Joint Ph.D.' (e.g. Statistics+ML, Neural Computation+ML) is NOT an admissions route — SCS verbatim: "Students interested in an ML-Joint Ph.D. should first apply to the Ph.D. program that best aligns with their research interests" and apply for the joint degree only after enrolling and passing 10-715, 10-705 and 10-716. CSD notes it "cannot... provide individualized feedback on your application." All SCS doctoral programs are full-time, in-person in Pittsburgh; no online/part-time options. No spring or summer entry.

faculty.rank: Alumni Research Professor of Computer Science; Director, Auton Lab
faculty.department: Robotics Institute, School of Computer Science
faculty.research_areas: Weak supervision and data programming, label-efficient learning, active/interactive labeling, machine learning for health and critical care, anomaly detection, time-series and survival analysis, ML for predictive maintenance
faculty.why_match: Akshat's SPIDER lumbar-spine result is a weak-supervision result in disguise: a U-Net teacher trained on only 54 labelled images (0.735 mIoU) produced confidence-filtered pseudo-labels that lifted a student to 0.816 mIoU (+8.1 points), and the per-class confidence thresholds calibrated on just 5 reference images matched those estimated from 304 — i.e. the labelling heuristic itself is cheap to learn. That is exactly the question Dubrawski's group asks in 'Interactive Weak Supervision: Learning Useful Heuristics for Data Labeling' (Boecking, Neiswanger, Xing, Dubrawski, ICLR 2021), which learns labelling functions from a small number of human interactions instead of assuming a fixed heuristic set. Akshat's negative result — that combining confidence thresholding with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty adds nothing over thresholding alone — is the kind of dependency-structure question the Auton Lab attacks head-on in 'Dependency Structure Misspecification in Multi-Source Weak Supervision Models'.
faculty.key_paper_1: Interactive Weak Supervision: Learning Useful Heuristics for Data Labeling — B. Boecking, W. Neiswanger, E. Xing, A. Dubrawski, ICLR 2021
faculty.key_paper_2: End-to-End Weak Supervision — S. Rühling Cachay, B. Boecking, A. Dubrawski, NeurIPS 2021 (see also 'Dependency Structure Misspecification in Multi-Source Weak Supervision Models' and 'Weak Supervision for Affordable Modeling of Electrocardiogram Data', all listed in the Auton Lab publication database)
faculty.taking_students: Unstated on an official page. Auton Lab is large, actively funded (incl. a $10.5M US Army predictive-maintenance contract) and continuously publishes with new student first-authors through 2025, so recruitment is near-certain — but no explicit 'I am taking students' notice was found (checked 2026-08-28).
faculty.contact_policy: not stated — no email restriction found. The Auton Lab site lists him directly under 'CONTACT US' with a phone number (412.268.6233) and a mailto link, which is an implicit invitation.
faculty.email_angle: I trained a U-Net teacher on 54 labelled spine MRIs and recovered +8.1 mIoU in a student from filtered pseudo-labels — but the confidence thresholds that did the work were calibrated just as well from 5 images as from 304, which made me want to read 'Interactive Weak Supervision' as a theory of why the labelling heuristic is the cheap part.
faculty.notes: AFFILIATION VERIFIED 2026-08-28: listed on the RI faculty directory as 'Artur W. Dubrawski — Alumni Research Professor of Computer Science'. Not emeritus, not on leave, no industry appointment found. CAVEAT: he is Robotics Institute, NOT MLD or CSD. Akshat's stated targets are the MLD and CSD Ph.D. programmes; to be advised by Dubrawski he would most likely need the RI Ph.D. (or a co-advising arrangement). Since one SCS application covers up to three doctoral programmes, adding the RI Ph.D. as a third choice is the cheap way to keep this door open. His RI profile page (www.ri.cmu.edu/ri-faculty/artur-dubrawski/) returns 404 as of this check — use the Auton Lab site instead. faculty.rank: Raj Reddy Associate Professor of Machine Learning; Director, Approximately Correct Machine Intelligence (ACMI) Lab
faculty.department: Machine Learning Department (courtesy appointments in Heinz College and Societal Computing)
faculty.research_areas: Distribution and label shift, learning with unlabelled data, data-centric ML and datapoint characterisation, robustness, representation learning and causality, clinical/medical ML, critical methodology of the field itself
faculty.why_match: Akshat's polyp study (Kvasir-SEG) held the architecture fixed and varied only preprocessing across three backbones: +0.045 Dice on U-Net, +0.058 on ResU-Net, but only +0.023 on Attention U-Net — the data intervention shrinks as representational capacity grows. That is a data-centric claim about which datapoints and which interventions actually carry signal, which is precisely the axis of 'Characterizing Datapoints via Second-Split Forgetting' (Maini, Garg, Lipton, Kolter, NeurIPS 2022), where forgetting dynamics separate mislabelled from merely-rare examples. Separately, Akshat's semi-supervised spine work leans entirely on unlabelled MRI slices, and Lipton's 'RATT: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Guarantee Generalization' (ICML 2021) is the formal version of the question he answered empirically. Method-identity fit is unusually strong: Lipton is the CMU faculty member most publicly committed to interrogating the field's own claims, which is exactly Akshat's stance (negative results, controlled ablations, testing untested assumptions).
faculty.key_paper_1: RATT: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Guarantee Generalization — S. Garg, S. Balakrishnan, J. Z. Kolter, Z. C. Lipton, ICML 2021
faculty.key_paper_2: Characterizing Datapoints via Second-Split Forgetting — P. Maini, S. Garg, Z. C. Lipton, J. Z. Kolter, NeurIPS 2022
faculty.scholar: not found on his homepage in this pass — homepage points to https://acmilab.org/ for the live publication list
faculty.taking_students: Unstated. His homepage says the site is deliberately static and refers visitors to the ACMI lab site for 'recent papers, current students, and other news'; acmilab.org would not render in this pass, so no admissions statement was confirmed (checked 2026-08-28).

Assistant: To maximize the likelihood that your email receives a response, please CC my administrative assistants: on the CMU side: Marlee Bandish (mbandish [at] andrew [dot] cmu [dot] edu), and on the Abridge side: Josh Fontanilla (josh [dot] fontanilla [at] abridge [dot] com)" — i.e. cold email is permitted but you MUST CC the assistants or expect no reply.
faculty.email_angle: In a controlled polyp-segmentation study I found the gain from a fixed preprocessing pipeline shrank from +0.058 Dice on ResU-Net to +0.023 on Attention U-Net — the data intervention substitutes for capacity — and I've been trying to work out whether that is the same phenomenon your Second-Split Forgetting paper isolates at the level of individual datapoints.
faculty.notes: MAJOR INDUSTRY APPOINTMENT — FLAG. His homepage states verbatim: "I am also the Cofounder & CTO of Abridge, a healthcare AI company." He maintains a CMU administrative assistant AND a separate Abridge assistant, which is a strong signal of divided availability. Weigh advising bandwidth accordingly. Still listed on the MLD core-faculty directory (verified 2026-08-28), so he has not departed. Both key papers were verified from an independent official CMU faculty publication list (zicokolter.com/publications) rather than from Lipton's own site, which is static; acmilab.org failed to render, so his most recent 2025-2026 output was not enumerated in this pass.

faculty.department: Machine Learning Department AND Department of Mathematical Sciences
faculty.research_areas: Generative modelling via stochastic interpolants, flow matching and flow maps, consistency models and self-distillation, diffusion theory, probability flows, generative models for science, few-step / one-step samplers
faculty.why_match: Akshat's DDPM pretraining study is a question about what a diffusion objective actually teaches an encoder: pretraining on unlabelled abdominal CT lifted liver Dice from 0.751 to 0.928, and a FROZEN encoder retained 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice — but the same frozen encoder on kidney fell BELOW random initialisation (0.654 vs 0.899). Boffi's 'Shallow diffusion networks provably learn hidden low-dimensional structure' (ICLR 2025) is the theoretical statement of exactly which latent structure a diffusion model can and cannot recover, which is the mechanism Akshat's per-organ split is groping toward empirically. His interest F (one-step generative models, distillation) maps directly onto 'How to build a consistency model: Learning flow maps via self-distillation' (NeurIPS 2025). Boffi is also a new assistant professor building a group, which usually means real advising time.
faculty.key_paper_1: Shallow diffusion networks provably learn hidden low-dimensional structure — N. M. Boffi, A. Jacot, S. Tu, I. M. Ziemann, ICLR 2025
faculty.key_paper_2: How to build a consistency model: Learning flow maps via self-distillation — N. M. Boffi, M. S. Albergo, E. Vanden-Eijnden, NeurIPS 2025 (see also 'Stochastic Interpolants: A Unifying Framework for Flows and Diffusions', JMLR 2025)
faculty.taking_students: Yes (implied, strong). His group page lists two current CSD PhD students, three MLD master's students, undergraduates and several affiliates, and states verbatim: "If you would like to work together, please don't hesitate to reach out — I am always open to pursuing new collaborations from within or outside CMU." No formal admissions statement, so this is inference from an active and growing group (checked 2026-08-28).
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM from his research-group page: "In addition to those I directly advise, I am fortunate to frequently collaborate with a talented set of students. If you would like to work together, please don't hesitate to reach out — I am always open to pursuing new collaborations from within or outside CMU." No restriction on prospective-student email. NOTE: his /applications page is about HIS faculty and postdoc applications (he posts his own research/teaching statements), not about applying to work with him — do not misread it.
faculty.email_angle: I pretrained a DDPM on unlabelled abdominal CT and found a frozen encoder kept 87% of fine-tuned liver Dice but fell below random init on kidney — reading 'Shallow diffusion networks provably learn hidden low-dimensional structure' made me suspect the split is about which latent structure the score actually identifies, not about organ difficulty.
faculty.notes: Verified on the MLD core-faculty directory and on his own site (2026-08-28). No industry appointment. Joint MLD + Mathematical Sciences appointment — a student could plausibly come in through MLD. CAVEAT: the group is mathematically heavy (stochastic interpolants, PDEs, JAX); Akshat has no theory publications, so an application here needs a credible signal of mathematical appetite, and the medical-imaging framing should be de-emphasised in favour of the 'what does the diffusion objective teach' question. Co-advising with Max Simchowitz, Andrej Risteski, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Albert Gu and Aditi Raghunathan is visible across his 2025-2026 preprints, so the network here is wide.

faculty.rank: Professor; leads the Neuro-Symbolic AI Group; co-Editor-in-Chief of JMLR
faculty.research_areas: Statistical machine learning for high-dimensional structured data, theory of representation learning and pretext tasks (contextures), graphical models, causal representation learning, neuro-symbolic methods for injecting domain knowledge and constraints, robustness to corruption and distribution shift
faculty.why_match: The single unresolved question in Akshat's DDPM work — why does a self-supervised prior transfer for liver (frozen encoder retains 87% of fine-tuned Dice) and actively hurt for kidney (0.654 frozen vs 0.899 random init)? — is the exact question Ravikumar formalises in 'Contextures: Representations from Contexts' (ICML 2025), which characterises the representation a pretext task/context induces and when that representation is the right one for the downstream task. On the other side, HiME imposes taxonomy structure by construction (per-level conditional sigmoids composed by the chain rule, so a child's probability cannot exceed its parent's, giving upward-closed prediction sets rather than post-hoc repair) — that is domain knowledge compiled into the decoder, and Ravikumar's group works the same seam from the other direction in 'Learning with Explanation Constraints' (Pukdee, Sam, Kolter, Balcan, Ravikumar, NeurIPS 2023) and 'Bayesian Neural Networks with Domain Knowledge Priors'. He is the CMU person who could turn Akshat's 'imposed vs learned structure' intuition into a theorem.
faculty.key_paper_1: Contextures: Representations from Contexts — ICML 2025 (listed as a Selected Publication on his CMU homepage)
faculty.key_paper_2: Learning with Explanation Constraints — R. Pukdee, D. Sam, J. Z. Kolter, M.-F. Balcan, P. Ravikumar, NeurIPS 2023 (see also 'Learning Interpretable Concepts: Unifying Causal Representation Learning and Foundation Models', NeurIPS 2024)
faculty.taking_students: Unstated. His group page lists four current PhD students (one joint with Nina Balcan, one joint with Zack Lipton) and three postdocs, with a long and steady alumni pipeline — an active, funded group, but no explicit admissions notice was found (checked 2026-08-28).
faculty.contact_policy: not stated — no email restriction on his homepage. Contact block lists his office (GHC 8111), his email in obfuscated form, and his administrative assistant (Christine Martik).
faculty.email_angle: I built a hierarchical classifier whose consistency is a theorem rather than a post-hoc repair, and separately found a diffusion-pretrained encoder that transfers for liver and fails below random init for kidney — 'Contextures' reads to me like the framework that would tell me in advance which of those two outcomes to expect.
faculty.notes: Verified on the MLD core-faculty directory and his own CMU page (2026-08-28). No emeritus/leave status. Two flags: (1) he lists an external venture, 'WoodWide AI', in his homepage contact block — not described as an employer, but note it; (2) as co-Editor-in-Chief of JMLR his service load is heavy. His homepage shows only three Selected Publications and defers to Google Scholar, so the 2026 output was not enumerated here. He co-advises with Lipton (Daniel Jeong) and Balcan, which is a useful route if Akshat wants both the theory and the data-centric side. NOTE: his older consistency-theory-for-multilabel work (with Koyejo, Natarajan, Dhillon) was NOT verified in this pass — do not cite it in an SOP without checking Google Scholar first.

faculty.rank: FORE Systems Professor; Director, NSF AI Institute for Societal Decision Making (AI-SDM)
faculty.research_areas: Interactive/feedback-driven learning: active sampling, experimental design, bandits, stochastic optimisation, reinforcement learning; statistically and computationally efficient data collection; human factors and RLHF; historically, semi-supervised learning theory
faculty.why_match: Akshat's most interesting semi-supervised finding is a data-selection result, not a segmentation result: per-class confidence thresholds estimated from 5 reference images matched those estimated from 304, and pushing to a fixed global threshold of 0.98 bought 0.938 pseudo-label IoU only by discarding ~17% of pixels — an explicit budget-versus-information trade-off. Singh's 'Near-Optimal Discrete Optimization for Experimental Design: A Regret Minimization Approach' (Mathematical Programming, 2021) is that trade-off stated as a selection problem: which small subset of measurements is sufficient. Her stated research goal on her CMU page is verbatim about "decisions about the most informative data and actions."
faculty.key_paper_1: Near-Optimal Discrete Optimization for Experimental Design: A Regret Minimization Approach — Mathematical Programming, 2021 (listed as a selected paper on her CMU homepage)
faculty.key_paper_2: Optimistic Algorithms for Adaptive Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect — ICML 2025 (listed on her CMU homepage)

faculty.notes: DEMOTED TO PARTIAL DELIBERATELY. Singh is historically the canonical CMU name for label-efficient and semi-supervised learning theory, but her CMU homepage's 'Selected recent papers' (updated with an AAAI'26 tutorial, so current) are now almost entirely reinforcement learning, bandits, treatment-effect estimation, RLHF and peer review — NOT semi-supervised learning or vision. Her page relegates 'past focus on learning and leveraging structure in data' to the full publication list. So the topical overlap with Akshat is real but historical; do not write an SOP paragraph implying she currently works on pseudo-labelling. Also note her AI-SDM directorship is a large administrative load. Verified on the MLD core-faculty directory 2026-08-28; no industry appointment found.

faculty.rank: Michael B. Donohue Associate Professor of Computer Science and Robotics
faculty.department: Robotics Institute (primary), with affiliated appointments in the Computer Science Department and the Machine Learning Department
faculty.lab: Generative Intelligence Lab (part of the CMU Graphics Lab and CMU Computer Vision Group)
faculty.research_areas: Generative models (GANs, diffusion), controllable synthesis, data attribution and provenance for generative models, synthetic data generation for downstream vision tasks, dataset distillation, model customisation and concept ablation, efficient / one-step generative models
faculty.why_match: Akshat's A-PDF work generates masks with a conditional WGAN-GP and then REFUSES to trust the discriminator, instead scoring generated images against the class-proportion distribution of real masks (Mahalanobis retains 33.7% of 5000 samples; kNN 35.1%) — i.e. an external, distributional quality filter on synthetic data. Zhu's lab asks the mirror-image question in 'Evaluating Data Attribution for Text-to-Image Models' (ICCV 2023), which builds the first serious evaluation of which training data a generated image is actually attributable to, and in 'Generating Multi-Image Synthetic Data for Text-to-Image Customization' (ICCV 2025). His lab explicitly lists 'Synthetic data generation with generative models: How can we use generative models to produce useful data for improving computer vision and robotics systems?' as a core question.
faculty.key_paper_1: Evaluating Data Attribution for Text-to-Image Models — S.-Y. Wang, A. A. Efros, J.-Y. Zhu, R. Zhang, ICCV 2023
faculty.key_paper_2: Differentiable Augmentation for Data-Efficient GAN Training — S. Zhao, Z. Liu, J. Lin, J.-Y. Zhu, S. Han, NeurIPS 2020 (see also 'Fast Data Attribution for Text-to-Image Models', NeurIPS 2025)
faculty.taking_students: Unstated for prospective PhD applicants. Six current PhD students are listed (RI, MLD, CSD) plus a steady MSCV/MSR pipeline, and 2026 output is heavy — an actively recruiting lab, but no admissions statement found (checked 2026-08-28).
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM from his homepage: "If you are a CMU student interested in our research, please fill out this inquiry form." (links to a Google Form). This is scoped to CURRENT CMU students; there is no stated policy for external prospective applicants, and no 'do not email me' notice. Practical read: as an external applicant, a short cold email is not prohibited but the form route is reserved for people already on campus.
faculty.email_angle: For a segmentation project I built a post-hoc filter that scores cWGAN-GP samples against the class-proportion distribution of real masks rather than trusting the discriminator — it throws away two thirds of them — and your data-attribution work is the closest thing I've found to a principled account of what a generated sample is actually worth.
faculty.notes: Verified on his own CMU page 2026-08-28; previously Adobe Research but that is prior employment, not a current joint appointment — no active industry role stated. PARTIAL, not Close, because the lab's centre of gravity is graphics, creative tooling and text-to-image control (BrickGPT won the ICCV 2025 Marr Prize; SIGGRAPH/CVPR/ICLR pipeline), NOT label-efficient learning, medical imaging or structured prediction. Akshat would be joining a synthesis lab and pivoting away from segmentation. Very competitive: alumni go to OpenAI, Roblox, MIT.

faculty.rank: Associate Professor (NSF CAREER 2023); co-director of the MS in Computational Biology programme
faculty.department: Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, School of Computer Science; courtesy appointments in the Robotics Institute and in Electrical and Computer Engineering
faculty.research_areas: Computer vision and machine learning for cellular cryo-electron tomography, unsupervised and weakly supervised 3D segmentation, few-shot and active learning for structure classification, diffusion/foundation-model features for biomedical imaging, saliency and explanation for medical images, embodied AI for autonomous labs
faculty.why_match: Akshat pretrained a DDPM on unlabelled abdominal CT and transferred the encoder to organ segmentation (liver Dice 0.751 to 0.928), then probed frozen features and found they retained 87% of fine-tuned liver Dice while collapsing below random init on kidney. Xu's 'Unsupervised Multi-Scale Segmentation of 3D Subcellular World with Stable Diffusion Foundation Model' (CVPR 2026, Highlight) does the same manoeuvre at scale — reading segmentation structure out of a diffusion model's features without labels — and would let Akshat test whether his per-organ failure is a property of the diffusion prior or of his 21-patient pretraining pool. His annotation-scarcity interest maps onto 'Weakly Supervised 3D Semantic Segmentation Using Cross-Image Consensus and Inter-Voxel Affinity Relations' (ICCV 2021) and 'Active learning to classify macromolecular structures in situ for less supervision in cryo-electron tomography' (Bioinformatics, 2021).

faculty.notes: DEPARTMENT MISMATCH — READ THIS BEFORE APPLYING. Xu is Computational Biology, not MLD or CSD. His own bio states he is 'training faculty at the Joint CMU-Pitt Ph.D. Program in Computational Biology' and training faculty for the MSCV programme. An MLD or CSD Ph.D. admit would NOT be routed to him by default; the direct routes are the CMU-Pitt Computational Biology Ph.D. (separate application at compbio.cmu.edu) or the RI Ph.D. via his courtesy RI appointment. Research fit is arguably the strongest on this entire sheet (diffusion features for segmentation + weak supervision + active learning + medical/bio imaging under annotation scarcity), so if Akshat is willing to widen the target beyond MLD/CSD, this is the highest-value addition. Verified affiliation, email and publication list on his own lab site 2026-08-28. No industry appointment. Note his domain is cryo-ET/microscopy, not radiology — the transfer of Akshat's CT/MRI experience is conceptual, not literal.

faculty.department: Language Technologies Institute AND Machine Learning Department, School of Computer Science
faculty.research_areas: CURRENT: likelihood-based generative reasoning (unifying diffusion/flow models with preference optimisation), agentic LLMs, generative retrieval, generative/unsupervised methods for combinatorial optimisation and PDE solvers, benchmarking. HISTORICAL: large-scale hierarchical and extreme multi-label text classification, taxonomy-structured prediction, text categorisation
faculty.why_match: HiME's contribution is that hierarchy consistency is a property of the decoding rule rather than a post-hoc repair — per-level conditional sigmoids composed by the chain rule give an upward-closed prediction set, verified across ViT-B/16, ViT-L/16, ResNet-50, ConvNeXt-T and EfficientNet-B0 at ~0.01% parameter overhead, reaching 95.8% decision-level accuracy on Galaxy Zoo 2 (239,573 images, 37 classes, 4 levels). Yang wrote the canonical CMU work on the alternative strategy — regularising a flat model toward the taxonomy rather than building the constraint in — in 'Recursive regularization for large-scale classification with hierarchical and graphical dependencies' (Gopal & Yang, KDD 2013, best student paper runner-up) and 'Bayesian models for large-scale hierarchical classification' (NIPS 2012). A direct comparison of Akshat's by-construction decoder against her recursive-regularisation baseline is a real, publishable experiment.

faculty.why_match: HiME's core move — making hierarchy consistency a structural guarantee of the decoder rather than something enforced afterwards, so the prediction set is upward-closed by the chain rule at ~0.01% parameter overhead — is the same design philosophy as Kolter's 'DC3: A learning method for optimization with hard constraints' (Donti, Rolnick, Kolter, ICLR 2021), which guarantees feasibility by completion-and-correction rather than by penalising violations, and as 'OptNet: Differentiable Optimization as a Layer in Neural Networks' (Amos & Kolter, ICML 2017). Akshat's other unresolved finding — that the structural constraint costs accuracy under a frozen encoder (0.858 vs a flat 0.888) but is free under full fine-tuning (0.952) — is precisely a constraint-versus-capacity question of the kind his group studies.

faculty.research_areas: AI for science, human-AI interaction, specialised models and agents, behavioural/interactive evaluation of ML systems; historically AutoML, neural architecture search, hyperparameter optimisation and reproducibility
faculty.why_match: Akshat's first paper is a controlled benchmark of U-Net variants for lung segmentation whose headline finding is a negative one — no variant is universally best — and the methodological identity behind it is 'test the assumption everyone skipped'. Talwalkar's 'Specialized Foundation Models Struggle to Beat Supervised Baselines' (Xu, Gupta, Cheng, Shen, Shen, Talwalkar, Khodak, ICLR 2025) is the same intervention aimed at a much larger target: a controlled study showing that the field's default assumption about pretrained foundation models does not survive a fair supervised comparison. His 'Efficient Architecture Search for Diverse Tasks' (Shen, Khodak, Talwalkar, NeurIPS 2022) is the constructive counterpart to Akshat's finding that architecture choice is task-dependent.
